title: Psycholinguistics
overview: Psycholinguistics connects language knowledge with mental processing, development and the brain. Begin with how people comprehend and produce language, then compare explanations of L1 and L2 learning, individual differences and patterns of language impairment.
journey: Observe the processes: comprehension, production and acquisition.
Trace development: early communication, words and increasingly complex patterns.
Compare explanations: biological, cognitive and social learning accounts.
Explain variation: age, motivation, memory, context and neural organisation.

topics.title: Psycholinguistics
topics.core: Psycholinguistics studies the mental knowledge and processes involved in acquiring, understanding and producing language.
topics.explanation: It examines how linguistic representations interact with attention, memory and other cognitive processes; mental processes are inferred from evidence rather than directly read from behaviour.
topics.example: Teaching example: A listener rapidly combines word meanings with sentence structure to understand a spoken question.
topics.confusion: Knowing grammatical rules explicitly is different from using tacit linguistic knowledge.

questions.prompt: Explain psycholinguistics briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: Psycholinguistics studies the mental knowledge and processes involved in acquiring, understanding and producing language.
questions.answer: Psycholinguistics studies the mental knowledge and processes involved in acquiring, understanding and producing language. It examines how linguistic representations interact with attention, memory and other cognitive processes; mental processes are inferred from evidence rather than directly read from behaviour.
keyPoints: Psycholinguistics studies the mental knowledge and processes involved in acquiring, understanding and producing language.

questions.prompt: Why can fluent speakers use a grammatical pattern without explaining its rule?
questions.shortAnswer: Much linguistic knowledge is tacit.
questions.answer: Much linguistic knowledge is tacit. Psycholinguistics distinguishes the representations that support use from a person's ability to state those representations consciously.
keyPoints: Much linguistic knowledge is tacit.
Psycholinguistics distinguishes the representations that support use from a person's ability to state those representations consciously.

topics.title: History of psycholinguistics
topics.core: Psycholinguistics developed through exchanges between psychology and linguistics, with a major mid-twentieth-century revival.
topics.explanation: Early work examined language and thought; behaviourist approaches stressed learning histories, while cognitive and generative work renewed interest in internal representations.
topics.example: Teaching example: The contrast between Skinner's account and Chomsky's critique helped shape debates about language learning.
topics.confusion: The field did not begin with one person or a single experiment.

questions.prompt: Why was the cognitive turn important for psycholinguistics?
questions.shortAnswer: It made internal representations and mental processes legitimate targets of explanation, encouraging experimental models of comprehension, production and acquisition beyond observable stimulus–response descriptions.
questions.answer: It made internal representations and mental processes legitimate targets of explanation, encouraging experimental models of comprehension, production and acquisition beyond observable stimulus–response descriptions.
keyPoints: It made internal representations and mental processes legitimate targets of explanation, encouraging experimental models of comprehension, production and acquisition beyond observable stimulus–response descriptions.

topics.title: Branches of psycholinguistics
topics.core: Psycholinguistic branches include experimental, developmental and neurolinguistic approaches to language.
topics.explanation: Experimental work studies processing through tasks; developmental work studies acquisition and change; neurolinguistics relates language to brain organisation.
topics.example: Teaching example: A child-language recording and an adult reaction-time experiment investigate different dimensions of language processing.
topics.confusion: The branches overlap rather than forming sealed disciplines.

questions.prompt: How can one study be both developmental and experimental?
questions.shortAnswer: It can compare children at different stages using a controlled language task.

topics.title: Speech production
topics.core: Speech production transforms a communicative intention into a planned and articulated utterance.
topics.explanation: A useful model distinguishes conceptualisation, formulation and articulation, with monitoring of the output. Real-time coordination is complex and partly automatic.
topics.example: Teaching example: A speaker chooses a message, selects words and grammatical patterns, then produces their sounds.
topics.confusion: An occasional speech error does not mean the speaker lacks the relevant grammar.

questions.prompt: What is speech production?

questions.prompt: What can a slip of the tongue reveal about production?
questions.shortAnswer: A systematic slip can show that speakers plan and organise linguistic units before articulation.
questions.answer: A systematic slip can show that speakers plan and organise linguistic units before articulation. The specific error pattern supplies evidence about representations and timing.

topics.title: Comprehension and context
topics.core: Comprehension builds an interpretation from linguistic input using knowledge and context.
topics.explanation: Listeners and readers identify forms, assemble structure and integrate meanings. Bottom-up input and top-down expectations can interact.
topics.example: Teaching example: The context of a river helps select the intended meaning of bank.
topics.confusion: Context can guide interpretation but does not make the acoustic or written input irrelevant.

questions.prompt: Why can the same word be recognised differently in different contexts?
questions.shortAnswer: Context activates different expectations and meanings, which interact with the incoming form.
questions.answer: Context activates different expectations and meanings, which interact with the incoming form. The listener must still connect that interpretation with the linguistic evidence.

topics.title: Pre-linguistic development
topics.core: Pre-linguistic development includes early perception, vocalisation and communicative behaviour before stable words.
topics.explanation: Infants attend to speech, participate in interaction and gradually tune perception to the languages around them. These abilities develop at varying rates.
topics.example: Teaching example: A baby alternates gaze and vocalisation with a caregiver before producing recognisable words.
topics.confusion: The absence of spoken words does not imply the absence of communicative learning.

questions.shortAnswer: It provides experience of coordinated communication, attention and response.

topics.title: Babbling
topics.core: Babbling is early production of speech-like syllabic patterns before stable meaningful words.
topics.explanation: Repeated and varied consonant–vowel sequences provide experience with articulation and interact with the ambient language. Babbling and later words show continuities and changes.
topics.example: Teaching example: Repeated ba-ba or varied ba-da are possible babbling patterns.
topics.confusion: A repeated sound becomes a word only when it has a sufficiently stable meaningful use.

topics.title: Sensori-motor development
topics.core: In Piaget's account, sensori-motor development concerns learning through perception and action during early life.
topics.explanation: Object permanence, intentional action and symbolic capacities provide a cognitive context for language development. Cognitive stages should not be treated as exact universal language timetables.
topics.example: Teaching example: A child searching for a hidden object shows an understanding relevant to representing absent things.
topics.confusion: Sensori-motor stage is a cognitive-development label, not a specific grammatical stage.

questions.prompt: How might object permanence support later language use?
questions.shortAnswer: Representing objects that are out of sight helps support reference beyond the immediate scene, though it does not by itself explain the acquisition of grammar.

topics.title: Holophrastic stage
topics.core: At the holophrastic stage, a single word can perform a communicative act that adults express more fully.
topics.explanation: Context, gesture and intonation help an adult interpret the intention; an adult paraphrase does not prove that the child represents a complete adult sentence internally.
topics.example: Teaching example: Milk may function as a request for milk, depending on the setting.
topics.confusion: One-word speech need not correspond to one fixed sentence meaning.

topics.title: Two-word combinations
topics.core: Two-word speech combines lexical items to express relationships such as agent–action or possession.
topics.explanation: Early combinations show emerging organisation, often without the full set of adult function words and inflections.
topics.example: Teaching example: Mummy go can link an agent with an action; daddy shoe can signal possession.
topics.confusion: Two adjacent words are not necessarily evidence of complete adult-like syntax.

questions.prompt: How can two-word speech reveal more than vocabulary growth?
questions.shortAnswer: The child combines words into meaningful relations and often uses language-appropriate ordering patterns, showing emerging structural knowledge rather than isolated naming alone.

topics.title: Telegraphic speech
topics.core: Telegraphic speech uses short multiword combinations with many content words but fewer function words or inflections.
topics.explanation: It can express increasingly varied meanings while grammatical detail continues to develop. The term describes a broad pattern, with substantial individual variation.
topics.example: Teaching example: Mummy give ball communicates an event while omitting several adult grammatical elements.
topics.confusion: Missing function words do not imply that the utterance lacks organisation.

topics.title: Overgeneralisation and the Wug test
topics.core: Overgeneralisation applies a learned pattern beyond its conventional range; novel-word tasks test productive knowledge.
topics.explanation: Children can use inflections on unfamiliar forms, supporting the idea that they generalise patterns rather than merely memorise all complete words.
topics.example: Teaching example: A child who says goed applies a regular past-tense pattern to an irregular verb.
topics.confusion: A developmental error can provide evidence of learning, not just failure.

topics.title: Caretaker speech
topics.core: Caretaker or child-directed speech is speech adapted to interaction with a child.
topics.explanation: It may involve exaggerated prosody, repetition, shorter utterances and responsive interaction, but its forms vary across cultures and contexts.
topics.example: Teaching example: A caregiver repeats a label while following the child's attention to an object.
topics.confusion: One culturally familiar style of baby talk is not a universal prerequisite for acquisition.

topics.title: Critical and sensitive periods
topics.core: A critical-period hypothesis proposes age-related constraints on language acquisition; sensitive-period accounts allow more gradual changes.
topics.explanation: Different language abilities may show different age patterns. Age-related outcomes interact with experience and learning opportunities, so a single rigid cutoff is too simple.
topics.example: Teaching example: Early and late learners may differ in ultimate pronunciation even when older beginners initially progress quickly.
topics.confusion: A decline in average attainment does not mean adults cannot learn a language successfully.

questions.shortAnswer: Age patterns can differ by skill, task and experience, and observational findings require interpretation.

topics.title: Deprivation evidence
topics.core: Language-deprivation cases inform age questions but contain major confounds.
topics.explanation: Severe isolation often involves trauma, poor care and uncertain developmental histories. Such cases cannot cleanly isolate age from every other influence.
topics.example: Teaching example: A late first-language learner's difficulties may reflect both timing and broader deprivation.
topics.confusion: One unusual case cannot by itself prove a universal biological cutoff.

topics.title: Behaviourist acquisition theory
topics.core: Behaviourist accounts explain language learning through environmental associations, imitation and reinforcement.
topics.explanation: Skinner's operant account emphasises consequences that shape verbal behaviour. It highlights input and learning history, while simple imitation struggles to explain productive novelty.
topics.example: Teaching example: A caregiver's response can reinforce a useful request, yet the child also creates unfamiliar utterances.
topics.confusion: Negative reinforcement removes an aversive condition; it is not the same as punishment.

questions.shortAnswer: Children normally hear went, not goed.

keyPoints: Children normally hear went, not goed.

topics.title: Mentalist and innatist theory
topics.core: Mentalist or innatist approaches propose that language learning depends partly on inborn linguistic capacities.
topics.explanation: Chomskyan accounts connect acquisition with Universal Grammar and the problem of explaining abstract knowledge from limited evidence. Particular formulations and empirical claims remain debated.
topics.example: Teaching example: Children learn structural dependencies that are not taught as explicit rules.
topics.confusion: Innateness does not mean learning occurs without linguistic experience.

questions.prompt: What does poverty of the stimulus argue, and what is debated?
questions.shortAnswer: It argues that some acquired knowledge exceeds what input alone straightforwardly explains, motivating innate constraints.
questions.answer: It argues that some acquired knowledge exceeds what input alone straightforwardly explains, motivating innate constraints. Researchers debate the input evidence, learning mechanisms and the nature of those constraints.

topics.title: Biological theory
topics.core: Biological accounts relate language acquisition to species-specific capacities, maturation and brain development.
topics.explanation: Lenneberg connected language development with biological timing. Modern interpretation requires attention to plasticity, distributed networks and continuing learning rather than an all-or-nothing developmental switch.
topics.example: Teaching example: Children's capacity to acquire accessible spoken or signed language shows biological preparedness interacting with experience.
topics.confusion: Biological contribution does not exclude social or cognitive explanation.

questions.shortAnswer: A capacity provides the ability to develop language, while accessible interaction and input shape which language and patterns are acquired.

topics.title: Cognitive acquisition theory
topics.core: Cognitive approaches connect language development with general processes such as categorisation, memory and pattern learning.
topics.explanation: Piagetian accounts emphasise links with conceptual development; other cognitive learning views focus on meaningful learning and information processing.
topics.example: Teaching example: A learner connects a new word to an existing concept and uses recurring patterns to extend its use.
topics.confusion: Cognitive approaches are a family of explanations, not one identical theory.

questions.prompt: What is cognitive acquisition theory?

questions.prompt: Why might meaningful learning help retain vocabulary better than isolated repetition alone?

topics.title: Social interactionist theory
topics.core: Social interactionist accounts explain acquisition through communication, joint activity and responsive support.
topics.explanation: Vygotskian approaches emphasise mediation and development through interaction; usage-based perspectives also examine how shared attention and recurring constructions support learning.
topics.example: Teaching example: A caregiver expands a child's request while maintaining the shared activity.
topics.confusion: Interaction is more than the physical presence of another speaker.

topics.title: Nature and nurture
topics.core: The nature–nurture debate concerns how biological preparedness and experience contribute to language development.
topics.explanation: Acquisition theories differ in what they treat as built in and which mechanisms they assign to learning. A useful comparison identifies the evidence each explains and its limits.
topics.example: Teaching example: Input supplies language-specific patterns, while human learners bring cognitive and biological capacities to that input.
topics.confusion: Showing that input matters does not settle exactly what is innate.

topics.title: Krashen's Monitor Model
topics.core: Krashen's Monitor Model proposes five hypotheses concerning acquisition, learning, monitoring, natural order, input and affect.
topics.explanation: The model distinguishes acquired competence from conscious learning and stresses comprehensible input. Its strong separation of learning and acquisition and the testability of its concepts have been criticised.
topics.example: Teaching example: A learner may know a rule explicitly yet fail to use it spontaneously in rapid conversation.
topics.confusion: Knowing a rule and using it fluently are different facts; that distinction alone does not prove the model's full claims.

topics.title: Acquisition, learning and monitoring
topics.core: In Krashen's account, acquisition is subconscious development and learning is conscious rule knowledge used for monitoring.
topics.explanation: Monitoring is proposed to require time, attention to form and knowledge of a rule. These conditions constrain its usefulness during spontaneous communication.

topics.confusion: The claim that conscious knowledge cannot become acquired competence is theoretically disputed.

questions.prompt: Why might a learner edit writing accurately but make similar errors when speaking quickly?

questions.answer: Editing permits time and attention to form, while rapid production draws on readily available processing. This difference is compatible with monitoring but does not uniquely confirm Krashen's whole model.

topics.title: Comprehensible input and affect
topics.core: Krashen proposes that acquisition is supported by comprehensible input beyond the learner's current level and facilitated by lower affective barriers.
topics.explanation: The notation i+1 is a conceptual description, not a simple measurable syllabus step. Input is important, while output, interaction and attention are also relevant in wider SLA research.
topics.example: Teaching example: A comprehensible story introduces a few unfamiliar forms in a meaningful context.
topics.confusion: Comprehensibility does not mean a text contains no new language.

keyPoints: Krashen proposes that acquisition is supported by comprehensible input beyond the learner's current level and facilitated by lower affective barriers.

questions.prompt: What is a limitation of using i+1 as an exact classroom formula?
questions.shortAnswer: The learner's i and the next step are difficult to specify precisely.

topics.title: Interlanguage
topics.core: Interlanguage is a learner's developing linguistic system, with patterns distinct from both the first language and target norms.
topics.explanation: It can be systematic, changing and variable across contexts. Selinker related its development to transfer, training, strategies, communication and overgeneralisation.
topics.example: Teaching example: A learner consistently omits third-person -s but changes usage as experience and context change.
topics.confusion: Learner language is more than a random collection of mistakes.

keyPoints: Interlanguage is a learner's developing linguistic system, with patterns distinct from both the first language and target norms.

questions.prompt: Why does a repeated learner error sometimes support an interlanguage analysis?
questions.shortAnswer: A regular pattern suggests a developing rule or representation.
questions.answer: A regular pattern suggests a developing rule or representation. Analyse where the form occurs and how it changes rather than treating each instance as unrelated failure.

topics.title: Linguistic universals
topics.core: Linguistic universals are proposed cross-linguistic properties or constraints, studied through typology and theories such as Universal Grammar.
topics.explanation: Typological approaches examine language samples and implicational patterns; generative approaches investigate constraints on possible grammars. L2 access to UG is a debated issue.
topics.example: Teaching example: A typological implication predicts that one structural property is associated with another across languages.
topics.confusion: A frequent cross-linguistic tendency is not automatically an exceptionless universal.

questions.prompt: Explain linguistic universals briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: Linguistic universals are proposed cross-linguistic properties or constraints, studied through typology and theories such as Universal Grammar.

keyPoints: Linguistic universals are proposed cross-linguistic properties or constraints, studied through typology and theories such as Universal Grammar.

questions.prompt: How do typological universals and Universal Grammar differ as approaches?
questions.shortAnswer: Typology infers patterns from comparisons of languages.
questions.answer: Typology infers patterns from comparisons of languages. Universal Grammar proposes constraints or principles of the language faculty; their explanations and methods differ.
keyPoints: Typology infers patterns from comparisons of languages.
Universal Grammar proposes constraints or principles of the language faculty; their explanations and methods differ.

topics.title: Acculturation theory
topics.core: Schumann's acculturation account links aspects of second-language development to social and psychological relations with the target-language community.
topics.explanation: Social distance, attitudes and opportunities for contact can constrain learning. The theory offers a contextual perspective but does not fully explain cognitive mechanisms or every classroom setting.
topics.example: Teaching example: A learner may have extensive residence but limited access to interaction with target-language users.
topics.confusion: Residence length does not automatically measure meaningful contact or social inclusion.

questions.prompt: What is acculturation theory?
questions.shortAnswer: Schumann's acculturation account links aspects of second-language development to social and psychological relations with the target-language community.

Social distance, attitudes and opportunities for contact can constrain learning. The theory offers a contextual perspective but does not fully explain cognitive mechanisms or every classroom setting.

questions.prompt: Why might years in an L2 environment fail to predict high proficiency?
questions.shortAnswer: Access, social distance, identity, work patterns and interaction opportunities differ.
questions.answer: Access, social distance, identity, work patterns and interaction opportunities differ. Time alone does not reveal the quality or range of language experience.
keyPoints: Access, social distance, identity, work patterns and interaction opportunities differ.
Time alone does not reveal the quality or range of language experience.

topics.title: McLaughlin's cognitive theory
topics.core: McLaughlin treats L2 learning as complex skill development involving controlled and increasingly automatic processing.
topics.explanation: Practice can reorganise knowledge and processing; restructuring can produce temporary performance changes. Attention is limited, so fluency involves efficient access rather than simply more explicit rules.
topics.example: Teaching example: An initially effortful pattern becomes easier to retrieve in a familiar communicative task.
topics.confusion: Automaticity is not identical to perfect accuracy or absence of meaning.

questions.prompt: What is mclaughlin's cognitive theory?
questions.shortAnswer: McLaughlin treats L2 learning as complex skill development involving controlled and increasingly automatic processing.
questions.answer: McLaughlin treats L2 learning as complex skill development involving controlled and increasingly automatic processing. Practice can reorganise knowledge and processing; restructuring can produce temporary performance changes. keyPoints: McLaughlin treats L2 learning as complex skill development involving controlled and increasingly automatic processing.

questions.prompt: How can a temporary performance decline occur during learning?
questions.shortAnswer: Restructuring can change an earlier system and temporarily disrupt performance.
questions.answer: Restructuring can change an earlier system and temporarily disrupt performance. A brief decline need not mean that no learning is taking place.
keyPoints: Restructuring can change an earlier system and temporarily disrupt performance.
A brief decline need not mean that no learning is taking place.

topics.title: Sociocultural theory and ZPD
topics.core: Sociocultural theory explains development through mediation and participation in social activity.
topics.explanation: The zone of proximal development concerns what learners can achieve with appropriate support beyond independent performance. Scaffolding should respond to need and be adjusted over time.
topics.example: Teaching example: A partner's prompt helps a learner complete an explanation they cannot yet produce alone.
topics.confusion: ZPD is not simply every task that is difficult.

questions.prompt: Explain sociocultural theory and zpd briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: Sociocultural theory explains development through mediation and participation in social activity.
questions.answer: Sociocultural theory explains development through mediation and participation in social activity. The zone of proximal development concerns what learners can achieve with appropriate support beyond independent performance. Scaffolding should respond to need and be adjusted over time.
keyPoints: Sociocultural theory explains development through mediation and participation in social activity.

questions.prompt: What distinguishes scaffolding from giving a learner the full answer?
questions.shortAnswer: Scaffolding supports the learner's own activity with contingent prompts or tools and can be reduced as independence grows.
questions.answer: Scaffolding supports the learner's own activity with contingent prompts or tools and can be reduced as independence grows. Supplying the answer may leave the learner's processing unchanged.
keyPoints: Scaffolding supports the learner's own activity with contingent prompts or tools and can be reduced as independence grows.

topics.title: Age and ultimate attainment
topics.core: Age can relate differently to initial learning rate and ultimate attainment.
topics.explanation: Older beginners may progress quickly in some instructed tasks, while earlier sustained exposure can favour later attainment in some domains. Experience, skill and context shape the pattern.
topics.example: Teaching example: An adult may learn classroom vocabulary faster initially while a child develops more target-like pronunciation over time.
topics.confusion: Younger is not automatically better on every measure at every stage.

questions.prompt: Explain age and ultimate attainment briefly.

questions.answer: Age can relate differently to initial learning rate and ultimate attainment. Older beginners may progress quickly in some instructed tasks, while earlier sustained exposure can favour later attainment in some domains. Experience, skill and context shape the pattern.
keyPoints: Age can relate differently to initial learning rate and ultimate attainment.

questions.prompt: Why distinguish rate from ultimate attainment when comparing child and adult learners?
questions.shortAnswer: A group can learn faster initially yet reach a different long-term outcome.
questions.answer: A group can learn faster initially yet reach a different long-term outcome. A short course and many years of exposure answer different age-related questions.
keyPoints: A group can learn faster initially yet reach a different long-term outcome.

topics.title: Language aptitude
topics.core: Language aptitude refers to abilities that help explain differences in the ease or rate of language learning.
topics.explanation: Classic components include phonetic coding, grammatical sensitivity, inductive learning and associative memory. Aptitude interacts with tasks and instruction.
topics.example: Teaching example: One learner quickly detects an unfamiliar grammatical pattern; another excels at remembering sound–word associations.
topics.confusion: Aptitude is not a total measure of a person's worth or a fixed guarantee of success.

questions.prompt: What is language aptitude?
questions.shortAnswer: Language aptitude refers to abilities that help explain differences in the ease or rate of language learning.
questions.answer: Language aptitude refers to abilities that help explain differences in the ease or rate of language learning. Classic components include phonetic coding, grammatical sensitivity, inductive learning and associative memory. Aptitude interacts with tasks and instruction.
keyPoints: Language aptitude refers to abilities that help explain differences in the ease or rate of language learning.

questions.prompt: How does aptitude differ from motivation?
questions.shortAnswer: Aptitude concerns abilities relevant to learning; motivation concerns goals, effort and persistence.
questions.answer: Aptitude concerns abilities relevant to learning; motivation concerns goals, effort and persistence. They can interact, but they are different constructs.
keyPoints: Aptitude concerns abilities relevant to learning; motivation concerns goals, effort and persistence.

topics.title: Attitude
topics.core: Attitude is an evaluative orientation toward a language, its users or the learning situation.
topics.explanation: Attitudes can influence engagement and be reshaped by experience and social context. Associations with success need careful causal interpretation.
topics.example: Teaching example: A learner's positive view of a classroom community may encourage participation.
topics.confusion: An attitude is not identical to proficiency or an observable amount of effort.

keyPoints: Attitude is an evaluative orientation toward a language, its users or the learning situation.

questions.prompt: Can successful learning change attitude as well as attitude influencing learning?
questions.shortAnswer: Yes.
questions.answer: Yes. The relationship can be reciprocal: experience and achievement may strengthen positive attitudes, while attitudes can affect engagement.
keyPoints: Yes.
The relationship can be reciprocal: experience and achievement may strengthen positive attitudes, while attitudes can affect engagement.

topics.title: Motivation
topics.core: Motivation concerns the direction, intensity and persistence of effort toward language-learning goals.
topics.explanation: Instrumental and integrative orientations concern reasons for learning; intrinsic and extrinsic distinctions concern the source or character of engagement. Motivation changes over time.
topics.example: Teaching example: A learner studies for employment and also enjoys communicating in the language.
topics.confusion: Instrumental reasons do not automatically produce weak learning.

questions.prompt: Can instrumental and intrinsic motivation coexist?
questions.shortAnswer: Yes.
questions.answer: Yes. A learner may want a qualification and also enjoy the activity itself. Motivational orientations can overlap and change with experience.
keyPoints: Yes.
A learner may want a qualification and also enjoy the activity itself.
Motivational orientations can overlap and change with experience.

topics.title: Personality, anxiety and willingness to communicate
topics.core: Personality-related factors and anxiety can affect participation and learning opportunities, with effects depending on task and setting.
topics.explanation: Extraversion may support some interaction, while introverted learners may succeed in other tasks. Willingness to communicate changes by topic, partner and perceived safety.
topics.example: Teaching example: A learner speaks freely with a friend but stays silent before an examiner.
topics.confusion: A quiet learner is not necessarily unmotivated or less capable.

questions.prompt: Explain personality, anxiety and willingness to communicate briefly.

questions.prompt: Why should an examiner-facing silence not be treated as proof of poor language knowledge?
questions.shortAnswer: Anxiety, processing pressure and the social setting can limit access or willingness to speak.
questions.answer: Anxiety, processing pressure and the social setting can limit access or willingness to speak. Performance reflects more than underlying knowledge alone.

topics.title: Cognitive style and learning-style claims
topics.core: Cognitive style describes habitual approaches to processing information; preferences do not establish that matching instruction to a style improves learning.
topics.explanation: Field dependence and independence are classic constructs in the guide. Measures overlap with other abilities, and style categories should not be treated as fixed prescriptions.
topics.example: Teaching example: A learner may prefer diagrams while still benefiting from explanations suited to the subject matter.
topics.confusion: Preference and demonstrated instructional effectiveness are different kinds of evidence.

topics.title: Memory and working memory
topics.core: Memory supports storage and retrieval of language; working memory maintains and manipulates information during ongoing activity.
topics.explanation: Phonological memory can support unfamiliar word forms, while meaningful connections and retrieval affect longer-term access. Capacity is task-dependent rather than a single explanation of success.
topics.example: Teaching example: A learner holds earlier words in mind while interpreting the end of a long sentence.
topics.confusion: Remembering a rule explicitly is not the same as accessing it efficiently in conversation.

questions.prompt: Explain memory and working memory briefly.

questions.shortAnswer: Maintaining and integrating its parts places processing demands on working memory and structural interpretation.
questions.answer: Maintaining and integrating its parts places processing demands on working memory and structural interpretation. Vocabulary familiarity alone does not remove those demands.

topics.title: Transfer and transfer of training
topics.core: Transfer uses prior knowledge in new learning; transfer of training concerns influences of previous teaching or practice.
topics.explanation: Similarity can support performance, while differences or learned routines can encourage non-target patterns. Not every learner error originates in L1.
topics.example: Teaching example: A repeatedly drilled answer format may be overused in conversation even where it is unnatural.
topics.confusion: L1 transfer and transfer of training have different sources.

topics.title: Intelligence and language learning
topics.core: Intelligence measures can relate to some language-learning tasks, especially academic and analytical ones, without explaining all communicative development.
topics.explanation: Different abilities and opportunities contribute to outcomes. Multiple-intelligences proposals should not be treated as proof that matching fixed learner types improves instruction.
topics.example: Teaching example: An analytic test score may relate to grammar study more directly than to comfortable conversation.
topics.confusion: A low score on one intelligence test does not imply inability to acquire or use language.

questions.prompt: Explain intelligence and language learning briefly.

questions.prompt: Why does an IQ score fail to provide a complete prediction of conversational proficiency?

topics.title: Fossilization and stabilisation
topics.core: Fossilization describes persistent stabilisation of interlanguage features despite opportunities for further development.
topics.explanation: Permanence is difficult to establish; a long-lasting pattern may change with new conditions. Distinguish a short plateau from stronger claims of fossilization.
topics.example: Teaching example: A learner persistently omits an inflection over many contexts and years.
topics.confusion: One repeated error or brief learning plateau is insufficient evidence of permanent cessation.

topics.title: Identity, investment and learner strategies
topics.core: Learner identity and access to valued activities shape how motivation can be put into practice.
topics.explanation: Investment relates participation to social identities and resources. Strategies include deliberate ways of organising learning or communication, whose effectiveness depends on task and context.
topics.example: Teaching example: An interested learner may speak little because peers exclude their contributions.
topics.confusion: Low participation is not always an individual motivational failure.

questions.prompt: How can a learner be motivated but have little chance to improve through interaction?
questions.shortAnswer: Social exclusion or unequal access can restrict participation despite strong desire.

topics.title: Neurolinguistics and lateralisation
topics.core: Neurolinguistics investigates relationships between language processes and brain organisation.
topics.explanation: Language is often left-lateralised, but multiple regions and pathways contribute; right-hemisphere processes can support prosody and discourse. Individual patterns vary.
topics.example: Teaching example: A language task can involve a network rather than one isolated point in the brain.
topics.confusion: Lateralisation does not mean one hemisphere performs all language alone.

questions.prompt: Explain neurolinguistics and lateralisation briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: Neurolinguistics investigates relationships between language processes and brain organisation.

questions.prompt: Why is left-lateralised language not equivalent to saying the right hemisphere has no role?
questions.shortAnswer: Lateralisation describes relative specialisation, not exclusive control.

topics.title: Aphasia
topics.core: Aphasia is an acquired language disorder associated with brain damage that can affect speaking, comprehension, reading or writing.
topics.explanation: Profiles vary with the affected network and individual history. Language impairment should not be equated with global loss of intelligence.
topics.example: Teaching example: A person may struggle to retrieve words after a stroke while retaining many other abilities.
topics.confusion: Aphasia is not simply a disorder of the speech muscles.

questions.shortAnswer: Aphasia is an acquired language disorder associated with brain damage that can affect speaking, comprehension, reading or writing.

questions.prompt: How can aphasia affect a person who can still move the speech organs?
questions.shortAnswer: The impairment concerns language representations or processing, such as word retrieval or comprehension, rather than only the motor ability to produce sound.
questions.answer: The impairment concerns language representations or processing, such as word retrieval or comprehension, rather than only the motor ability to produce sound.

topics.title: Broca-type and Wernicke-type profiles
topics.core: Classic Broca-type aphasia often involves effortful nonfluent production; Wernicke-type profiles often involve fluent but impaired meaningful communication and comprehension.
topics.explanation: These are useful historical clinical patterns, not perfectly separate language boxes. Symptoms and lesion locations do not map one to one in every individual.

topics.title: Dyslexia
topics.core: Dyslexia involves persistent difficulty with accurate or fluent word reading and related literacy processes.
topics.explanation: Developmental and acquired reading difficulties should be distinguished. Phonological processing often matters, while profiles vary; intelligence alone does not define reading skill.

topics.title: Language therapy
topics.core: Language therapy aims to support communication by restoring skills where possible and developing compensatory strategies.
topics.explanation: Intervention follows assessment of the individual's needs and goals and may involve family, educational or clinical support. Outcomes vary and improvement can continue beyond an early recovery phase.
topics.example: Teaching example: Practising word retrieval and using communication aids can address different functional needs.
topics.confusion: Language therapy is not one universal drill for every language difficulty.

questions.prompt: Why should therapy goals be individualised rather than based only on a diagnostic label?

topics.title: Brain imaging and behavioural methods
topics.core: Neurolinguistic research combines behavioural evidence with methods that examine brain structure or activity.
topics.explanation: MRI can show anatomy; functional methods examine task-related signals; EEG and event-related potentials provide fine temporal information. Each method has limits of inference.

questions.prompt: Explain brain imaging and behavioural methods briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: Neurolinguistic research combines behavioural evidence with methods that examine brain structure or activity.
questions.answer: Neurolinguistic research combines behavioural evidence with methods that examine brain structure or activity. MRI can show anatomy; functional methods examine task-related signals; EEG and event-related potentials provide fine temporal information. Each method has limits of inference.
keyPoints: Neurolinguistic research combines behavioural evidence with methods that examine brain structure or activity.

questions.prompt: Why combine reaction-time evidence with a brain measure?
questions.shortAnswer: They provide complementary observations about performance and neural processes.
questions.answer: They provide complementary observations about performance and neural processes. Converging evidence can constrain an explanation more effectively than interpreting either measure alone.
keyPoints: They provide complementary observations about performance and neural processes.
Converging evidence can constrain an explanation more effectively than interpreting either measure alone.

topics.title: Plasticity and modularity
topics.core: Plasticity concerns change in brain organisation; modularity concerns the degree to which language processes are specialised.
topics.explanation: Recovery and developmental adaptation show flexibility, while dissociations suggest partially distinguishable abilities. Neither observation requires completely isolated, fixed modules.
topics.example: Teaching example: Different patterns of impairment can help distinguish word retrieval from other cognitive abilities.
topics.confusion: A dissociation supports a distinction but does not automatically prove total independence.

questions.prompt: Why can a dissociation between language and another ability be informative without proving an isolated language organ?
questions.shortAnswer: Different performance patterns suggest separable components or demands.
questions.answer: Different performance patterns suggest separable components or demands. The tasks may still depend on interacting networks, so stronger anatomical and theoretical claims require additional evidence.
